{{expand French|Algorithme d'Atlantic City|category=Articles needing translation from French Wikipedia|date=June 2022}}

{{Short description|Type of randomized algorithm}}

In computing, an '''Atlantic City algorithm''' is a [[randomized algorithm]] that answers correctly at least 75% of the time<ref name="BachShallit1996">{{cite book |last1=Bach |first1=Eric |last2=Shallit |first2=Jeffrey |date=1996 |title=Algorithmic Number Theory, Volume 1: Efficient Algorithms |location=Cambridge |publisher=MIT Press |page=51-52 |isbn=0-262-02405-5}}</ref>. In some variant definitions, the correctness threshold may be any value greater than 50%<ref name="Mollin2003">{{cite book |last=Mollin |first=Richard |date=2003 |title=RSA and Public-Key Cryptography |location=Boca Raton |publisher=Chapman & Hall/CRC |page=80 |isbn=1-58488-338-3}}</ref>. In either sense, Atlantic City algorithms are types of [[Monte Carlo algorithm|Monte Carlo algorithms]].

There exists a polynomial-time Atlantic City algorithm for any problem belonging to the class [[BPP (complexity)|BPP]] of bounded probabilistic polynomial-time problems<ref name="BachShallit1996"></ref>.

[[Las Vegas algorithm]]s, which never return an incorrect answer, are a [[dual (mathematics)|dual]] of Monte Carlo algorithms and, therefore, of Atlantic City algorithms.

The name refers to [[Atlantic City, New Jersey|Atlantic City]] in the [[U.S. state]] of [[New Jersey]]. Much like [[Monte Carlo]] and [[Las Vegas]], Atlantic City is widely associated with casinos and gambling culture.
